options.label: We'll do it.
options.tooltip: Leave it to us: a Dragon, a Founder and a Loaf, by sunset.

nodes.text: There you are: the troupe! Hedda Brask. I keep The Bell, and every year I direct the Founders' Play, here on the square, at sunset. Which is today. We have a stage. We do not have a Dragon, a Founder or a Loaf. Lady Agathe won't come down from the castle. Sanna, the net-mender, has run off to her aunt's lighthouse. And Oskar, the baker, can't bake, because Runa, the smith, has his oven door.
Of course you're the troupe. You walked onto my square on the right afternoon with nothing to do. That is what a troupe is. Now, are you going to stand there, or are you going to help?

The founding of Kelderby, in three scenes, always in this order. First the Founder: a fisherwoman sails into the bay. Then the Dragon: it comes down the mountain and says she may stay if she brings it one loaf a year. Then the Loaf: she bakes the first Mountain Loaf, the Dragon eats it and becomes the town's friend, and everyone goes to the tavern. The tavern isn't in the play. It's still true.

The Dragon is up at the castle, at the top of the long road from this square. The lighthouse is out on the headland: down the main street, along the lane near the bottom, then the cliff path. The bakery is just below the square, and the smithy is halfway down the main street, under the anvil sign.
Still here? The sun isn't waiting. The Dragon is up at the castle, the Founder is out at the lighthouse, and the Loaf is somewhere between the bakery and the smithy. I'll hold the square.
She has played the Dragon for thirty years. She is my oldest friend and she roars like a landslide. If she says she won't come down, there's a reason, and it won't be the one she sent.
Sanna mends nets on the quay and knows every line of the Founder. She says them perfectly to the gulls. Faces are another matter.
They have been arguing since they were nine. Runa mended Oskar's oven door, and now she won't give it back until he admits something he will never admit. Bread is involved. Mostly it's pride.
Places! Places, everyone. The benches are filling and the sun is going down. The moment I have a Dragon, a Founder and a Loaf on this square, the curtain goes up. Have I?
Then go and get them! I will hold the sun. I won't, but I will glare at it.
The curtain goes up on a painted sea. Sanna steps out as the Founder, opens her mouth, sees two hundred faces, and stops. The whole square waits. She looks at you.

Sanna finds the front row: four carved pumpkins, grinning on a bench. She talks to them, and she talks to them so well that the square forgets she ever stopped. 'I have crossed the cold sea,' she tells the pumpkins, 'and I mean to stay.'

Sanna's hands start mending a net that isn't there, and the speech comes out as the work-song every net-mender on the quay knows. By the second verse the fishwives on the benches are singing it with her.
You whisper the line from the wings. Sanna says it after you, loud and clear, and then the next one without you. 'I have crossed the cold sea, and I mean to stay.'
Thunder on a sheet of tin. The lanterns along the stage flicker. The Dragon comes down from the mountain.
Lady Agathe sweeps on in the whole costume, tail and all, and roars like a landslide. Up in the castle courtyard, in the box you nailed up, a jackdaw sleeps through it.

Lady Agathe sweeps on, and behind her, wrapped in sailcloth, Dumpling floats in as the tail. The children in the front row scream with joy. Lady Agathe roars, and Dumpling, who has never heard her roar, hums louder.
You roar from the wings. Lady Agathe turns and roars back at you, twice as loud, and the square applauds the contest before the Dragon remembers the play.
'Bring me my loaf!' roars the Dragon. The Founder turns to the wings, and the baker comes on with the Mountain Loaf.

Oskar carries the Mountain Loaf on in both arms, golden from his own oven with its own door. The Dragon takes one bite, then another, and then, against every rehearsal, the whole loaf. 'Friends,' says the Dragon, with its mouth full. That is the end of the play.

Runa carries the Mountain Loaf on, black as a horseshoe and twice as heavy. The Dragon bites. The Dragon's teeth do not. Lady Agathe tries again from the side. Somebody in the third row laughs, then everybody, and the play stops right there, one scene short of its end.

options.label: Take a bow.
options.tooltip: Step out in front of the whole town and bow.

options.label: Wave the letter.
options.tooltip: Hold up the troupe's letter, delivered a week ago to the wrong door, so the whole square sees it.

nodes.text: Hedda walks to the front of the stage and speaks to the benches, and to you. 'Kelderby, I have a confession. The troupe I hired never came. These are not actors. I knew it the moment they walked onto my square, and I said nothing, because they said yes. Give them a hand.'
Three scenes. You'll have it on the programme like everybody else. Lady Agathe has kept every programme since the first; ask her steward to show you, he'll pretend he knows where they are.
Curtain? What curtain? Have you seen the sunset? Look at that sunset. Somebody should paint it. Not me. I'm busy. With the sunset.
Ah. You found that. Well. Keep it in your pocket until the curtain call, would you? I have a speech, and it's better if you've read the letter.

options.label: Take us to her.
options.tooltip: We'll find the costume and talk to the lady.

nodes.text: Visitors. Good afternoon. Bernt, steward. The lady is in the great hall and is not coming down, she says, though she has had her coat brushed. The costume? The Dragon's Head, a grinning thing of painted canvas; the Dragon's Wings, a pair of green silk ones; and the tail. I packed them away after last year's play, in three places I thought very sensible at the time.
In the kitchen, in the trunk by the great hearth. Dragons like to be warm. So do I. That is why I chose it.

In the royal apartments upstairs, in the old trunk with the candle latch. My lady's grandmother made it: three candles in three of the lady's rooms, and the latch gives when they are lit in the order the play is told. Light one out of turn and it simply won't take. The order? I never could keep it. My lady keeps every programme the play ever had, framed, in the lord's hall.
Drying on the wall walk. With a lodger in it. You will see. I would rather not be the one who tells the lady what you see.

happening.subject: npc/agathe
happening.text: The nest goes to a box in the courtyard and the Dragon has its whole tail back.

options.label: Move the nest
options.tooltip: Carry the nest, eggs and all, to a box in the courtyard, and Lady Agathe wears the whole costume.

happening.subject: npc/dumpling
happening.text: Dumpling becomes the Dragon's tail, and the jackdaw keeps her house.

options.label: Dumpling as the tail
options.tooltip: Leave the nest where it is. Dumpling floats behind her in sailcloth, and he is the tail.

nodes.text: Hedda sent you, and you have found my head and my wings, I see. Sit, there's tea. Here is the trouble: a jackdaw has built her nest in the Dragon's tail and laid in it, and I will not turn a neighbour out of her house on the afternoon of a play. And here is the other trouble: I am seventy-eight, I am afraid I am too old to be a dragon, and I would rather not find out in front of the whole town.

Dragons are old. That is rather the point of them. But a dragon is supposed to come down a mountain, and I am not sure my knees agree. I have been afraid of it since spring. There. I've said it, and you may tell Hedda, and she will shout.
She came in through the window in March and chose the tail, because it is green and warm and full of wicker. Very sensible. She has four eggs. I have not named them yet.

My ghast, the big white one by the ceiling. He floats about the castle and hums. He follows me everywhere, which is lovely, and into the bath, which is not. He would follow me down to the square in a heartbeat, if anyone thought to ask him.
I am down early to frighten the children while they're fresh. Tell Hedda the Dragon has come. Tell her I said I was afraid, too. She'll like that.
You found those. Thirty of them. 'First time. Terrified. Roared anyway.' I wrote that. I had forgotten I was ever terrified. Well. Perhaps I'll be terrified again tonight, and roar anyway.
Dumpling hums at you, low and contented, and turns slowly so you can admire all of him.
Dumpling, wrapped in sailcloth from end to end, hums at you. He has never been a tail before. He seems to think it is going well.

options.label: We'll find them.
options.tooltip: Four pumpkins, somewhere in the lower town. We'll bring them back.

nodes.text: Inga, lighthouse. My niece is in the lamp room and won't come down. She rehearses to an audience of pumpkins she carved faces into, and the harbour children have run off with every one of them for a lark. No audience, no rehearsal, no Founder.

The children leave chalk riddles; they can't help it. They play on the harbour quay, round the fishmonger's yard, by the chandler's, and down at the cottages past the cooper's lane. The pumpkins won't be hard to see. They have faces.

happening.subject: npc/inga
happening.text: Inga accepts the party's apology for the harbour children.

options.label: We were wrong.
options.tooltip: We named the children too quickly. We'll say so to Elin as well.

nodes.text: You told the weaver my harbour children stole her curtain. They're kept in now, the lot of them, the night of the play. They borrow pumpkins. They do not steal curtains.

happening.subject: npc/sanna
happening.text: The carved pumpkins will sit in the front row for Sanna.

options.label: Pumpkins in front
options.tooltip: The pumpkins go down to the square and sit in the front row, and Sanna speaks to them.

happening.subject: npc/sanna
happening.text: Sanna will sing the Founder's lines as the net-mending song.

options.label: Make it a song
options.tooltip: Turn the Founder's speeches into the net-mending song. Her hands know it already.

nodes.text: Oh! People. Faces. Hello. You brought them back! All four. 'I have crossed the cold sea—' sorry. I'm the Founder. I know every line right up until somebody looks at me, and then I know nothing at all. Two hundred faces on that square. These four are fine. They're pumpkins.
They don't blink. They don't whisper to the person next to them. They don't know my mother. I carved the faces so they'd feel like an audience, and then I made them all look pleased.
'I have crossed the cold sea in a boat no bigger than a door, and I mean to stay.' See? Fine. Now look at me. No, look at me. Gone. All of it. Even the door.

Chamomile, honey, and somebody you trust where you can see them. The apothecary's sign. Aunt Inga will be in the gallery. I could look at her. I could look at you. That's two. Two is nearly an audience.

happening.subject: npc/oskar
happening.text: The Mountain Loaf goes into Oskar's own oven with its own door.

options.label: Bake in your oven
options.tooltip: Hang the door back on, fire the oven, and bake the Mountain Loaf the way it has always been baked.

happening.subject: npc/runa
happening.text: The Mountain Loaf goes into Runa's forge.

options.label: Bake in Runa's forge
options.tooltip: Runa swears her forge does it in four minutes. Take the dough down the street and let her.

nodes.text: Oskar, baker. The recipe's on the board, if you can read it through the flour. Spring water off the castle road, honey from the bee garden, and an oven with a door on it. I have an oven. Runa has the door.

She mended it. Beautifully. And then laid it on her bench by the forge like a trophy, and says I can have it back when somebody admits a forge bakes better than an oven. I will not. You might. I won't watch.
The spring is beside the castle road, at the first bend above the square. The bee garden is further up, past the herder's sheep. Runa is halfway down the main street, under the anvil.
It's in. It's baking. Don't open anything. Don't look at anything. Go up to the square and tell Hedda the Loaf is coming.

options.label: Forges bake better
options.tooltip: Say it, out loud, where the street can hear: a forge bakes better than an oven.

happening.subject: npc/runa
happening.text: Runa gives the door back, reminded that Oskar mended her bellows for nothing.

options.label: Your bellows...
options.tooltip: Oskar mended your bellows last winter and wouldn't take a penny. It's in your own ledger.

happening.subject: npc/runa
happening.text: Runa trades the door for news of her lost lucky horseshoe.

options.label: We found your shoe
options.tooltip: Your lucky horseshoe is nailed under the herder's eaves up the castle road. The news, for the door.

options.label: We have the door.
options.tooltip: Look at your bench. We lifted it while you were at the anvil.

nodes.text: Come for the door, have you? Beautiful door. I mended it. Best thing in my forge. Oskar can have it back the moment somebody admits that a forge bakes better than an oven. Not him, even. Anybody. I'm not proud.
Hotter. Faster. A loaf in an oven takes an hour. A loaf in my forge takes four minutes. What comes out is a loaf. Mostly. You can knock with it.

options.label: We'll find them.
options.tooltip: Three singers, by sunset. Leave it to us.

options.label: They're coming!
options.tooltip: Kettil, Mari and Sverre all said yes. Warm up.

nodes.text: Fenna, tavern. A shanty is four voices and I have one: mine. Kettil sings only where nobody can see him. Mari won't sing till she hears her note. And Sverre waits to be asked properly, by his whole name, which nobody remembers.

Kettil's at the cooper's: listen for him, don't look for him. Mari's in the net loft by the water; there's a bell in her yard. Sverre's in the boatwright's shed, building a boat with his name on it, which is the only place anybody's written it down.

A curtain? I saw a big blue bundle go up the street at dawn, towards the square. Somebody was carrying it who walked like they were late for something. With a pencil behind their ear. I thought it was laundry.
The potter painted that for Kettil. He sings it in the tub, every verse. If you heard him, you heard the best bass in Kelderby. Don't tell him. He'll stop.
Kettil. Cooper. Busy. Don't watch me hoop. I do a lot of things better when nobody's looking.
Sing? Me? With people looking? No. Absolutely not. Where would I even— no.
You lifted the lid. Nobody lifts the lid. Fine. I'll sing. From the back. Behind a barrel. Don't look.
That pot is a lie. Mostly. All right, I sing it in the tub. The tub has very good sound. Everybody's voice is better in a tub.
Mari! Net loft! Up on the high bit, me, always. Ha! Only I can't find it cold. I need the note first, from something that rings true. Nothing in this town rings true except the bell in my yard.
If somebody rings my bell, I'll find my note, and if I find my note I'll be on that square by sunset. Ha! Go on. It's right there.
Hm. Sverre. Boatwright. Fenna wants me, does she. Fenna can ask. Properly.
Sverre what? Nobody in this town knows the rest of my name. Eleven years. It's written down in exactly one place, and I'm standing next to it.

options.label: We'll find out.
options.tooltip: Leave it with us. We'll look for clues and ask around.

options.label: Hedda took it.
options.tooltip: It was Hedda. It must have been.

options.label: Hedda, to measure
options.tooltip: Hedda took it to measure it against the fire lane: her pencil on your frame, your blue on her inn's bench, her playbill in the by-law book.

happening.subject: npc/vidar
happening.text: Elin is told the clerk took her curtain, and believes it.

options.label: Vidar took it.
options.tooltip: The clerk who said it blocks the fire lane. Who else?

happening.subject: npc/inga
happening.text: Elin is told the harbour children took her curtain, and believes it.

options.label: The harbour kids.
options.tooltip: The harbour children took the pumpkins. Why not a curtain?

nodes.text: Elin, weaver. My new curtain for the play, red and gold, nine hundred threads to the hand, was on that drying frame at midnight. At dawn: gone. Pegs and all. Find out who took it, and tell me, and I'll be out of that door with a broom.

Vidar Foss said it would block the fire lane, and he's been looking at me sideways all week. The harbour children take anything that isn't nailed down. And Hedda keeps asking how long it is, and I keep telling her: long enough.
Vidar! Of course! Clerks! She is already leaning out of the window, shouting it down the street towards the guildhall, where everyone can hear. Somewhere down the street, a door slams.
The harbour lot! I'll tell Inga! She is out of the door before you can stop her, and back a minute later, out of breath. 'Inga's keeping them in tonight. Was it them, though? Are you sure?'
Vidar Foss, clerk to the guild. By-law nine: four paces clear of anything that burns, every way out of the square. I said so about the weaver's curtain and I will say so again.

I objected to it. I did not abduct it. I was here at dawn, copying out by-law nine, and found the book gone from the cathedral already. Somebody else was reading up on the fire lane before breakfast. Draw your own conclusions. I have.

options.label: We were wrong.
options.tooltip: We named you too quickly. We were wrong, and we'll tell Elin so.

nodes.text: I have been accused of curtain theft from a window, in front of the guild, by name. I have it in writing. Somebody wrote it down for me.
